drug_class: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody / Disease-modifying therapy for multiple sclerosis
purpose: Ocrelizumab is used to treat multiple sclerosis (MS), including both the relapsing forms and primary progressive MS. It helps slow down how fast the disease gets worse and reduces the number of MS attacks (relapses). It is one of the few treatments approved for primary progressive MS, which is harder to treat.
how_it_works: Your immune system has certain white blood cells called B-cells that mistakenly attack the protective coating around your nerves in MS. Ocrelizumab works by targeting and reducing these harmful B-cells, which helps protect your nerves from damage. Think of it like removing the troublemakers from your immune system so they can no longer hurt your nerves.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are infusion reactions during or after the IV treatment, such as itching, rash, flushing, fatigue, low blood pressure, or throat irritation. You may also have a higher chance of getting infections like colds, respiratory infections, or urinary tract infections. These are usually manageable and your care team will monitor you closely.
warnings: Because this medication lowers certain immune cells, you are more at risk for serious infections, including a rare but serious brain infection called PML. You should not get live vaccines while on this medication. It can also reactivate hepatitis B, so you will be tested before starting. There is a potential increased risk of certain cancers, particularly breast cancer, so regular screenings are important. Always tell your doctor about any signs of infection.
typical_dosing: Ocrelizumab is given as an IV infusion at a clinic or infusion center. The first dose is split into two infusions given two weeks apart. After that, you receive one infusion every six months. Each infusion takes about 3.5 hours or longer, and you will be watched for at least an hour afterward to make sure you feel okay.
